generatedProse.concept-context: In academic study, integrating sources means using them to support your argument, not reporting them one after another. The weaker habit lists what each source says, so the paragraph reads as a summary of the reading. The stronger habit puts your point first and brings sources in to back it, qualify it, or set up a contrast. The voices technique keeps your own voice in charge: you state the point, bring in supporting and contrasting sources, then close with your own judgement.
generatedProse.worked-example:
Consider two students writing a paragraph that draws on the same four sources.

{{learner-a}} writes: one source made a claim; another said something similar; a third noted a different pattern; a fourth qualified the point. Each sentence reports a source, in the order they were read. The paragraph is accurate, but it has no point of its own. The reader learns what four authors said, not what the writer makes of it. This is reporting.

{{learner-b}} opens in their own voice with the paragraph's point, then brings the sources in to serve it: a supporting source, a second that reinforces it, then a contrasting source that complicates the picture. They close in their own voice with a short judgement that weighs them. The same four sources now support an argument. This is the voices technique.

Both students used the sources. Only {{learner-b}} kept their own voice in charge of the paragraph.
generatedProse.summary: Integrating sources, in any subject, means using them to support your argument rather than reporting them. The voices technique keeps your own voice in charge: you state the point, bring in supporting and contrasting sources, then close with a judgement. You can now tell using a source from reporting it, and arrange several voices in a single paragraph. The next lesson sharpens this into a critical edge.

check.body: In the worked example, how did {{learner-b}} weave the four sources into one paragraph?

items.text: Their own voice first, then supporting and contrasting sources, then a closing judgement.
By reporting each source in turn in the order they were read.
By removing the contrasting source so the point looked stronger.
By quoting all four sources at length with no comment.

feedback.correct: That's right. {{learner-b}} led in their own voice and arranged supporting and contrasting sources around it.
feedback.incorrectNotFinal: Not quite. Look for the option where the writer's voice frames the sources.
feedback.incorrectFinal: {{learner-b}} opened in their own voice, brought in supporting and contrasting sources, and closed with a judgement. The others report, cut or quote.
